I have to disagree with the author on the points of privacy and AI - the people designing the software behind these things have already had those ethical debates. The people designing self-driving cars right now are asking themselves as they design the software "Should this lead to an accident, who should be considered at fault? If I see a person in the middle of the road, do I swerve to avoid them even if it kills me? What if there are school children on the sidewalk and swerving would kill several of them?" even though as the self-driving car's AI is designed, it will obey all traffic laws to the letter and therefore many of these scenarios are highly unlikely.

I work in a branch of the pharmaceutical industry, and when writing validations for the software we offer to state governments, we have to ask ourselves if it is better to deny a drug to a patient based on a lack of documentation and save the state money, or if we should err towards approving the drug and possibly saving a life.

Furthermore, on the subject of privacy, it's been proven in several studies that simply looking at the metadata that a person generates is more than enough to track them and predict their next moves ahead of time - being able to look into all of the data collected on one's personal device only obfuscates the bigger picture, not only because there is more data to look through, but because when looking through a large data set, it's possible to get too concentrated on the minutiae of one's personal life and miss other clues that can lead to the bigger picture.
